content.text: Pay & salaryNASA Astronaut Salary: How Much Do They Earn? What is an astronaut?Astronaut salariesAstronaut career path and advancement opportunitiesThe Expanding frontier of space careersImage descriptionAn astronaut stands in a spacesuit next to text that reads: Astronaut SalariesCivilian astronaut salaries range from $104,898 to $161.141 per year.Military astronauts pay depends on their active duty status for pay, leave, benefits and other military matters.Becoming a NASA astronaut is one of the most competitive and prestigious career paths in the world. These highly trained professionals command, pilot, or serve as crew members on missions that advance space exploration and scientific discovery. Whether conducting research aboard the International Space Station (ISS) or maintaining critical spacecraft systems, NASA astronauts play a vital role in expanding humanity’s reach beyond Earth. Each selection cycle is extremely competitive, with thousands of applicants vying for just a handful of spots in NASA’s intensive astronaut selection program.Astronaut positions are highly competitive; only a few positions are available to those who have the right experience and meet NASA’s physical and mental qualifications. How much an astronaut earns will depend on their employment status and rank in the military or their expertise as a civilian.In this article, we take a look at what an astronaut does, note their average salary and answer some frequently asked questions about this esteemed career path.What is an astronaut?A NASA astronaut is a highly trained expert who participates in missions related to space exploration, spaceflight, and scientific advancement. These individuals command, pilot, or serve as crew aboard spacecraft—most notably to the International Space Station (ISS)—where they conduct research, test new technologies, and support long-duration missions beyond Earth. The astronaut selection process is extremely competitive, requiring candidates to meet physical and mental standards, demonstrate advanced education in STEM fields, and complete years of specialized training. Candidates may apply as civilian astronauts or military astronauts, depending on their background.NASA astronauts are tasked with maintaining spacecraft systems, performing zero-gravity physical training, executing repairs on satellites, and coordinating international collaborations in space. Their work spans both mission-critical operations and high-profile public appearances for media and educational outreach. Whether conducting experiments in aerospace medicine, supporting communications systems, or preparing for extended stays in low-Earth orbit, astronauts are essential to NASA’s broader objectives. While on Earth, they train at facilities such as Johnson Space Center in Houston, gaining proficiency in SCUBA diving, survival scenarios, robotics, and ISS systems. Along with technical ability, astronauts must exhibit strong critical-thinking skills, self-discipline, and adaptability—all essential for high-pressure environments and isolated conditions.Related: 21 In-Demand STEM Careers (Plus Duties and Salaries)Astronaut salariesA NASA astronaut’s salary is based on education and experience level. They bring home good pay, but you may be surprised to learn that, due to such high demand for such few positions, astronauts are not paid as much as professional athletes or movie stars.CivilianThe pay grades for civilian astronaut candidates are set by federal government pay scales and vary based on academic achievements and experience. According to NASA, civilian astronaut salaries range from $104,898 to $161,141 per year.Here are a few of the benefits offered to civilian astronauts:Health careTravelPaid holidaysChallenging and interesting workState-of-the-art training facilitiesPaid leaveMilitaryMilitary astronauts are designated to the Johnson Space Center in Houston and their pay depends on their active duty status for pay, leave, benefits and other military matters. Military astronaut candidates typically are commissioned officers with a minimum of five years of active duty service. The monthly military pay scales are represented in these tables.Military astronaut benefits include those above as well as monthly housing allowances and aviation career incentive pay.Related: 16 Top Space Industry Jobs To ConsiderFrequently asked questionsWhat are the basic requirements to become a NASA astronaut?To qualify for the NASA astronaut program, candidates must:Be a U.S. citizenHold at least a master’s degree in a STEM field such as engineering, mathematics, physical science, computer science, or biological scienceAccumulate a minimum of two years of relevant professional experience or 1,000 hours of pilot-in-command time in jet aircraft (for pilots)Successfully pass the NASA long-duration spaceflight physicalDemonstrate strong leadership, teamwork, and communication skillsHow much do NASA astronauts make?The astronaut salary for civilian candidates ranges from $104,898 to $161,141 per year, depending on education, pay grade, and years of experience. Military astronauts are compensated based on their active duty rank and receive additional military benefits, such as housing allowances, aviation incentive pay, and retirement perks.What is the difference between military and civilian astronauts?Civilian astronauts are federal employees and paid under the General Schedule (GS) pay scaleMilitary astronauts remain under Department of Defense pay grades, with rank-based salaries and extra active duty benefitsBoth undergo similar spaceflight training and may serve together on missions to the International Space Station (ISS)How long do astronauts stay in space?Astronauts on long-duration ISS missions typically stay in space for about six months, though some may remain up to a year. These extended stays help with research on the long-term effects of microgravity on the human body and contribute to future space exploration goals, such as missions to the Moon or Mars.Do astronauts receive overtime pay?As federal employees, civilian astronauts generally do not receive overtime pay. Their compensation includes base salary, benefits, and per diem for travel. Military astronauts are also not eligible for overtime, but may receive incentive pay for aviation or hazard conditions.Are there different types of astronauts?Yes. NASA astronauts are typically categorized as:Pilot astronauts – responsible for spacecraft operationMission specialists – focus on conducting scientific research, spacewalks, and operating ISS systemsPayload specialists – usually researchers or engineers from partner agencies or private companies like SpaceX or BoeingCan astronauts work for private space companies?Yes, NASA astronauts and astronaut candidates can transition to careers with private space companies, which are playing a growing role in the future of space exploration. Leading aerospace companies such as SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Boeing are developing commercial spacecraft and launching missions to the International Space Station (ISS) and beyond. These companies often recruit experienced astronauts for technical consulting, mission planning, and commercial spaceflight operations. Former military astronauts and civilian astronauts may also contribute to spacecraft testing, astronaut training programs, and spaceflight simulation development. What skills do astronauts need? NASA astronauts require a broad range of skills to thrive in the challenging and unpredictable environment of spaceflight. Whether working aboard the International Space Station (ISS) or preparing for future space missions with private space companies like SpaceX or Boeing, successful astronaut candidates must demonstrate advanced critical-thinking, adaptability, and the ability to work under extreme conditions—including zero gravity and long-duration isolation. In addition to strong communication and teamwork, astronauts benefit from technical knowledge in aerospace systems, robotics, and engineering. These skills are essential not only for mission success, but also for collaboration with international partners and ground-based space agency teams.Astronauts need a variety of skills to be successful in their positions. Some skills they should possess are: Advanced intelligence To excel as a NASA astronaut, candidates must demonstrate far more than just academic success in STEM fields—they need a high level of cognitive flexibility, intellectual curiosity, and the capacity to solve complex, often life-threatening problems in real time. During astronaut training, individuals face intense simulations that test their ability to make mission-critical decisions under pressure. Whether navigating technical malfunctions aboard the International Space Station (ISS) or responding to unexpected anomalies during spaceflight, astronauts rely on sharp problem-solving abilities and multidisciplinary expertise. This includes applying principles from physics, biology, engineering, and space research to rapidly assess situations and take decisive action. The combination of analytical thinking and creative reasoning helps astronauts adapt to the unique and evolving demands of deep-space exploration. Adaptability Astronauts should be able to adapt quickly when they are required to move from one task to another. They must be willing to adjust to new procedures and standards that are implemented. They also work with professionals from various industries in different countries, so they should be able to easily acclimatize to other environments and cultures. Mental endurance Astronauts may have to live in close quarters with other people for months at a time and experience long periods of time away from their families. They should be of sound mind and be able to cope with the trials they may face in their careers, including fear and isolation. Physical stamina Astronauts are required to pass spaceflight physical fitness tests. They must also pass a military water survival test, which tests the ability to tread water while wearing flight gear and to swim a certain distance without stopping. Astronauts also need to be SCUBA-qualified to prepare for underwater spacewalk training. They will be subjected to varying atmospheric pressures and their bodies must respond well. They also need to be prepared for the effects of zero-gravity. Critical-thinking skills Astronauts have difficult problems to solve and they must evaluate their work and the work of others in a careful and critical manner to ensure each task is completed correctly. Self-discipline When astronauts go into space, they need the self-discipline to work alone and live aboard the space station and accomplish their assigned tasks at their due time. Related: Soft Skills: Definitions and Examples Upgrade your resume Showcase your skills with help from a resume expertAstronaut career path and advancement opportunitiesBecoming a NASA astronaut is often the pinnacle of a highly specialized career in aerospace, military service, or STEM research. Before selection, most astronaut candidates have extensive experience as engineers, scientists, pilots, or medical doctors. After completing the rigorous astronaut training program, candidates become eligible for assignment to spaceflight missions, including travel to the International Space Station (ISS).Career advancement in the space agency can include leadership roles such as capsule communicator (CAPCOM) at Johnson Space Center, mission director, or even chief astronaut, a role responsible for training and assigning crews. Some astronauts move into high-profile administrative roles within NASA, contribute to space policy, or become educators and public figures promoting space exploration.Additionally, many retired astronauts transition into careers with private aerospace companies like SpaceX, Boeing, or Blue Origin, where their expertise helps shape the future of commercial spaceflight. Others write books, give keynote speeches, or serve on advisory boards, continuing to inspire future generations of explorers and innovators.The Expanding frontier of space careersAs space exploration grows increasingly commercialized, more NASA astronauts are finding opportunities beyond the national aeronautics and space administration. Companies like SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Boeing—leaders in aerospace innovation—have begun recruiting astronaut candidates for new roles supporting the international space station (ISS) and future spaceflight missions. Former military astronauts, experienced in active duty environments and high-stakes operations, are especially valued for missions involving extended stays in low Earth orbit. The astronaut selection process for private missions remains competitive, but these roles offer alternative career paths for professionals with a background in engineering, piloting, or science.The ISS continues to be a hub for research and operations, requiring personnel skilled in equipment maintenance, incidentals management, and coordination with international partners. As space agencies collaborate globally, astronauts must possess the adaptability and endurance to manage missions lasting months away from Earth. Individuals with years of experience in STEM fields, particularly those with prior service as federal employees or specialists from institutions like the Johnson Space Center in Houston, are uniquely positioned for these roles. Whether aboard a Starliner capsule or collaborating on space travel technology, modern astronauts are shaping the future of life beyond Earth.While your chances of becoming an astronaut are low, there are a variety of careers within the space industry.
